backups.overview: Mount Seattle (6,246 ft) rises deep in the Olympic interior, about 7.5 miles southeast of Mount Olympus, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Its northeast aspect drops over 3,800 ft to the Elwha valley in only about 1.5 miles, but the standard scramble routes stay on the gentler south/west scree and talus slopes. The peak was named April 29, 1890 by James Halbold Christie and topographer Charles Adams Barnes of the Seattle Press Expedition, in honor of the city that sponsored their winter crossing of the range; it was first climbed in 1907 by Asahel Curtis, Grant Humes, and Lorenz Nelson while reconnoitering for a climbing club's first attempt on Mount Olympus. Reaching the base of the peak requires a long, committing wilderness approach from either the Elwha or North Fork Quinault drainages — there is no easy day-trip line to this summit.
backups.beta: Most parties base-camp at Seattle Meadows (~4,550 ft), reached via a multi-day approach up the North Fork Quinault River to Low Divide and then west into Seattle Creek Basin. From camp, climb scree slopes on the mountain's western side, cross over a ridge, and continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, finishing with a class 2-3 scramble on the east ridge/side to the craggy summit. Two other approach variants exist (via Noyes Basin, and a more direct line up Seattle Creek Basin itself), converging on the same upper-mountain scramble.
backups.turnaround: Because the upper mountain is loose scree/talus with real rockfall and slip potential, and the approach is long and entirely off-trail through remote wilderness, set a firm turnaround time before starting the summit push and commit to it — visibility loss (fog/cloud) on the unmarked upper slopes is the biggest threat to a safe descent, and there is no faster way down than the way up.

backups.pro_needs: No technical protection is documented for this route — it is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no glacier travel per the published route description.
backups.approach: Two realistic approach corridors exist, both multi-day: (1) North Fork Quinault side — from the North Fork Quinault Trailhead at the end of the North Shore Road (not the South Shore Road, which leads to Graves Creek and the East Fork instead), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail or the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge Primitive Trail (via Three Lakes and Kimta Peak) to Low Divide, 16 miles one-way by the river trail and much farther by the ridge, then cross-country/climbers'-path to Seattle Meadows below the peak's south side. (2) Elwha side — from the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road to it has been closed to vehicles at Madison Falls since November 2017 flood damage, adding about seven miles each way on foot or bike), follow the Elwha River Trail up the Elwha valley toward Elwha Basin/Low Divide (on the order of 20+ miles one-way), then leave trail to climb into Seattle Creek Basin or Noyes Basin on the peak's northeast side. Either way, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp, with several thousand feet of trail gain before any scrambling begins. The Seattle Creek Basin approach (Elwha side) follows the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, forcing a steep, brushy bushwhack up onto the Mt. Noyes-Mt. Seattle ridge — expect slow going in heavy brush low down.
backups.descent_text: Descend the ascent line in reverse: downclimb the east ridge scramble back to the scree/talus on the east side, cross back over the connecting ridge, and descend the west-side scree to Seattle Meadows camp. The scree and talus are loose and unconsolidated in places, so downclimb carefully rather than trying to glissade or boot-ski except where lingering early-season snow makes it safe; rockfall onto parties below is a real concern on the looser sections.
backups.bail: Reverse the scramble; no fixed anchors required.

access.fees: Olympic NP wilderness permit reservation: $6 reservation fee plus $8 per person per night for climbers/backpackers age 16+ (15 and under free), as of 2026.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Hard-sided, approved bear-resistant food canisters are required for all overnight stays throughout most of Olympic Wilderness, including the Elwha and Quinault interior zones; bear wires/hangs are not accepted. There is no separate climbing registration — rangers do not certify competency or refuse a permit for lack of gear/experience, so self-sufficiency and route knowledge are entirely on the party.
access.permit: A backcountry wilderness camping permit is required for any overnight stay and must be reserved through recreation.gov before your trip.
access.closures: Olympic Hot Springs Road beyond Madison Falls has been closed to vehicles since November 2017 flood damage, with no reopening date on Olympic National Park's alerts page updated August 27, 2026, adding roughly 7 miles each way of walking or biking to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead on the Elwha approach. On the Quinault side, South Shore Road has a separate washout closure near milepost 8 (use North Shore Road as the detour); North Shore Road itself also had a seasonal construction closure near milepost 10.2 (culvert replacement, closed July 9–Sept 22, 2025). Call the park's Road and Weather Hotline (360-565-3131) or check nps.gov/olym for current status before committing to either approach.

approach_variants.baseFinding: The staging point is Seattle Meadows, the high camp in upper Seattle Basin about a thousand feet above Seattle Creek. There is no gully mouth to find here: from camp the climb starts on scree on the mountain's western side, and the base is simply where meadow gives way to loose scree and the slope steepens. What identifies the route is the sequence, so hold it in mind — climb the west-side scree, cross over a connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, and finish with Class 2 to 3 scrambling on the east ridge to a craggy top. If you are still high on the west side and the ground is cliffing out above you, you have failed to make the crossing and need to traverse. The summit is confirmed by an unusually large plastic tube jammed into a crack holding the register. Coming instead up Seattle Creek Basin, follow the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, then take the steep brushy bushwhack onto the Noyes–Seattle ridge; that brush low down is the crux of that variant, not the scrambling above.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

backups.approach: Follow the same approach as the other two summits: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Saddle Lake (2.5 mi) and Goat Flats (~4.5 mi) to Tin Can Gap (~6.2-7 mi), then drop ~400 ft off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier and cross it (moat and possible crevasse hazard — crampons/axe recommended, rope up if crevasses are open). Most parties bivy on or near the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing all three summits car-to-car. From a glacier-side camp, Middle Peak's south face is reached by a short climb/traverse toward the base of the peak; one detailed trip report logged the summit in about 37 minutes from a glacier bivy. The route itself is solid 3rd- and 4th-class scrambling on the lower face, transitioning to looser, more broken 3rd-class rock higher up — take care with rockfall onto anyone below, and expect the climbing to run longer than the peak's modest height suggests since the face is broader than it looks from the glacier. No technical rock gear is required for the standard line, but a rope is worth carrying for the optional short rappel on descent (see below) and in case conditions call for a belay on the looser upper section.
backups.descent_text: Middle Peak is primarily downclimbed by reversing the ascent line — most parties report no fixed rappel is needed, picking a careful line down through the looser upper 3rd class rock and the sounder 3rd/4th class below. Some parties do choose a short single-rope rappel (natural anchor — a horn, block, or sling around a chockstone/tree; no bolted anchors reported) to bypass the loosest or most exposed step on the upper face, particularly with larger groups or when downclimbing feels riskier than descending on the rope; a single 30m or half a 60m rope is plenty for this. After regaining the glacier-side camp/route, reverse the glacier crossing (mind the moat), climb back to Tin Can Gap, and follow Trail #641 out via Goat Flats and Saddle Lake. Loose rock on the upper face is the main descent hazard — helmet strongly recommended — along with the same glacier moat/crevasse considerations shared with the other two summits.

approach_variants.baseFinding: From the glacier-side camp, this summit's SOUTH FACE is reached by a short climb and traverse straight to the foot of the peak — and the discriminator against its northern neighbour is the absence of a col: you do NOT gain a saddle first and you do not climb a thousand feet on the far side of the glacier before touching rock. If you have gained a col, you are on the wrong tower. The face is BROADER than it looks from the ice, so pick the line from the glacier before you start up; the lower rock is solid third and fourth class and it turns looser and more broken higher, which is the confirmation you are on the described line rather than a cleaner variation. Negative markers: if you are following a ramp leftward into a shallow chimney out of a saddle, you are on the northern tower's route; if you are under three stacked wooden ladders pinned into the rock, you are at the lookout summit at the far southern end of the ridge.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap high camp
bivy.notes: The last flat ground before the glacier, roughly a mile short of the lookout, and the correct camp for a party that wants the summit block early and cold rather than soft. The maintained trail effectively ends here, so everything above is a bootpath, snow and the ladders. Its value is that it puts the glacier crossing and the ladders in the first hour of the day, when the snow is still firm — a real advantage over starting from the meadows two miles back. The cost is exposure: it is a gap, it catches weather, and there is nothing sheltering about it. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin vegetation, and take a hard look at whether the crossing above is in condition before committing to a camp that only makes sense if you go up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only for most of the season, and nothing at all once the snow around the gap has gone. Assume you are melting or carrying from Goat Flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit required. Federal recreation pass to park. Campfires prohibited on this whole stretch of trail; there is no fuel here regardless.
bivy.capacity: A few small pitches on rock and snow at and just below the gap; one or two parties, not a group site

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.
bivy.water: Reliable through most of the season from the tarns and small streams in the meadows, though the standing water is shallow and warms up late in summer. Treat everything. Later in a dry year the tarns shrink and the better water is the running melt above the flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
bivy.capacity: The main camping area on this approach — several established pockets spread through the meadows and around the tarns. It absorbs a fair number of parties but is genuinely crowded on summer and autumn weekends, and it is the overflow when the lookout is full.

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.
bivy.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation

backups.overview: A long, storied outing to the historic fire lookout perched on the South Peak of Three Fingers, crossing the Queest-Alb Glacier. The L-4 gable lookout was built 1930-1932 by Darrington-area mountaineers Harold Engles and Frank Benesh (with Harry Bedal having assisted in the 1929 feasibility scout), staffed seasonally from 1933 through 1942, later rebuilt by volunteers, and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1987 — roughly the top 15 feet of the summit block was blasted flat to seat the cabin. It remains one of the most iconic hike-scrambles in the Cascade foothills, thanks largely to the three vertical ladders cabled to the final summit tower.
backups.beta: This is the line Harry Bedal, Harold Engles, and Frank Benesh used to reach the South Peak summit to build the fire lookout in the early 1930s, and it remains the standard way up. From the trailhead the route follows trail to Saddle Lake, Goat Flats, and Tin Can Gap, then crosses the edge of the Queest-Alb Glacier before a rock scramble and a set of three fixed ladders (rebar and timber anchored into steep rock) gain the summit block and lookout. It is popular as a long day trip or, more commonly, an overnight from Goat Flats or Tin Can Gap given the approach length.

backups.best_season: August through mid-September is the classic window, but ice axe is essentially mandatory all season and crampons/a rope are strongly recommended for any attempt before September, when the Queest-Alb Glacier is icier and the moat bypass isn't yet open.
backups.approach: From the Tupso Pass trailhead, follow Three Fingers Trail #641 through forest to Saddle Lake (~2.5 mi, last easy water — no fires or camping within 200 ft of the lake past this point), then continue up through meadows to Goat Flats (~4.5 mi total), a broad subalpine bench with the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail climbs roughly 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2-7 mi total, most of the day's 4,200 ft gain banked); this is where the maintained trail effectively ends and most casual hikers turn around. Beyond the gap, drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier — a short but real glacier crossing with a moat between ice and rock that widens through the season (crampons/axe strongly recommended, especially before August); a rope is worth carrying if crevasses are open. On the far side, scramble up rock and snow past the base of the summit block to the historic lookout's ladder system: three fixed wooden ladders bolted/pinned into the rock, stacked in sequence, gaining the final class-5-equivalent rock band to the lookout deck. The transition between the second and third ladder is the trickiest move and is awkward with a full pack; exposure is significant and a slip here would be serious, so this last pitch is why the route is rated a scramble rather than a hike despite no rope typically being used. Some parties fix or find a hand-line/rope on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier — treat it as unverified fixed gear.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no roped rappelling on the standard line. Downclimb the three fixed ladders in reverse (facing in, one at a time, mind the awkward 2nd-to-3rd ladder transition), then reverse the rock/snow scramble back down to and across the Queest-Alb Glacier, watching the moat and any open crevasses. Climb back up to Tin Can Gap and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. The main descent hazards are the exposed ladder pitch (a fall here would be very serious despite no technical rappelling), a soft or icy glacier moat later in the day, and lingering steep snow on the south ridge in early season — an ice axe is recommended into mid-summer. No rappel gear is needed for the standard route.
backups.bail: Retreat to Tin Can Gap/Goat Flat; no shortcut descent.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Goat Flats Trailhead (via Tupso Pass Road FS 41/FS 4160)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: East-northeast from Mountain Loop Highway milepost 7; FS Road 41 then FS 4160 approximately 17.5 miles

approach_variants.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
approach_variants.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.
hazards: moat between glacier and rock that widens through the season and is hard to enter in poor visibility
crevasses on the Queest-Alb once it opens up
exposure on the ladders, particularly between the second and third
unverified fixed hand-line on the rock step past Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the MOAT between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the SOUTH peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.

approach_variants.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
approach_variants.notes:
FR 41 has washed out repeatedly and the closure point has moved. Reported blockages have been around five miles up from the Mountain Loop Highway, and at other times past the Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.
approach_variants.season: whenever the road is closed at the washout
hazards: several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish
all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail
approach_variants.baseFinding: Once you reach Tupso Pass the route is identical, and the same markers apply: cross to the north side of the ridge past Tin Can Gap to meet the top of the Queest-Alb, find the moat entrance rather than stepping onto open ice, and finish on the three stacked ladders on the SOUTH peak.

climbing_route.label: Short exposed rock step past Tin Can Gap
climbing_route.notes: Some parties fix or find a hand-line/rope on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap, before the glacier — treat it as unverified fixed gear.

climbing_route.label: Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier crossing
climbing_route.notes: Beyond Tin Can Gap, drop off-trail onto the glacier — a short but real crossing with a moat between ice and rock that widens through the season. Crampons and axe strongly recommended, especially before August; a rope is worth carrying if crevasses are open.

climbing_route.label: Rock and snow scramble to the ladders
climbing_route.notes: On the far side of the glacier, scramble up rock and snow past the base of the summit block to the historic lookout's ladder system.

climbing_route.label: Three fixed wooden ladders to the lookout deck
climbing_route.notes: Three fixed wooden ladders bolted/pinned into the rock, stacked in sequence, gain the final rock band to the lookout deck. The transition between the second and third ladder is the trickiest move and is awkward with a full pack; exposure is significant and a slip here would be serious, which is why this last pitch makes the route a scramble rather than a hike despite no rope typically being used.

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.notes: The main camp for the peak, an open subalpine meadow on a ridge crest a little over two miles beyond Saddle Lake and roughly two and a half miles short of the lookout, with a view west to Puget Sound. Bears work the area, so bring a canister or another way to secure food.
bivy.water: Tarns only — there is no running water at the flats, and the tarn water has been described as stale by autumn. The last dependable running water is a stream well below, around the 4,200 ft mark; above the flats the next water is glacier and snow melt beyond Tin Can Gap. Late in a dry season, plan to carry from low down.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Boulder River Wilderness. Campfires are prohibited in the Goat Flats area outright, and also anywhere within a quarter mile of Trail 641 above Saddle Lake. No overnight permit or quota is published. There is a backcountry toilet at the flats; note that it must not be used for packed-out waste bags.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites spread across the meadow, and it is regularly crowded on summer and autumn weekends. Camp only on ground that is already bare — the meadow is fragile and the Forest Service asks for existing sites only.

bivy.name: Three Fingers Lookout
bivy.notes: A 1930s fire lookout on the South Peak that climbers sleep in, reached by ladders with serious exposure — decide for yourself whether the final block is safe on the day. The door is never locked, but in winter and spring it can be frozen, swollen or buried, and the summit block itself is hard to climb then; summer is the season for it. Bring a tent as a fallback: it fills on good weekends and visitation is heavy even midweek. accounts disagree on whether there is usable ground to camp outside — some say pitch below the lookout, others say there is nowhere safe on the summit at all — so do not count on it.
bivy.water: None at the site — there is no potable water at the lookout and nothing to melt but snow.
bivy.permit: No fee, no reservation and no permit — it is open to whoever reaches it first. There is no toilet: carry a waste bag and pack everything out, and do not put it in the Goat Flats toilet or leave it below the lookout. The volunteers who maintain the building ask that you take crampons off before going in, keep the shutters closed in bad weather and when you leave, leave nothing behind, and not force shutters that are locked.
bivy.capacity: Maximum occupancy of eight, first come first served. Accounts of the actual floor put it nearer three or four people plus two more on the sleeping platform, so eight is a squeeze rather than a plan. Arrive early or expect to be turned away by whoever got there first.

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.notes: Two and a half miles in from Tupso Pass on a rough, root-bound forest trail — the first water and the first flat ground, but low and far from the mountain. Volunteers built a shelter at the meadow edge here in the early 1970s; no current source confirms it still stands or is usable, so do not plan on sleeping in it.
bivy.water: The lake — there is no running water here, and in a warm year it has been reported shrinking and buggy by mid-summer.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Boulder River Wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 200 ft slope distance of the shoreline of Saddle Lake and of Bandana Lake, and campfires are prohibited within the same 200 ft of both. No trailhead permit or quota is published for this trail, and the wilderness is closed throughout to pack and saddle stock.
bivy.capacity: Not published. It is a small four-acre lake and the setback rule below pushes camps back off the water.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap
bivy.notes: The last ground before the climbing starts: the Forest Service names it Tin Pan Gap, most climbers say Tin Can Gap, and it is where the route stops being a walk and starts needing equipment and judgement. accounts disagree on the distance in, from roughly six to eight miles, so do not plan a turnaround time off one figure. Useful mainly to parties who want a short summit morning on the glacier.
bivy.permit: The campfire closure along Trail 641 above Saddle Lake extends here.
bivy.capacity: A few spots at the gap and at the foot of the snow slope below it — small, and second choice to Goat Flats.

backups.name: North Peak
gear: Rope and a small rack (slings, small cams/nuts) for the chimney and rappels
Ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach
Extra webbing for building 2 rappel anchors
Helmet
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the North/Middle col
Loose rock in the chimney/ramp system
No established trail or cairned route — routefinding is on you
Committing rappel descent with only fixed-anchor slings of unknown age at some stations
backups.overview: Contrary to this route's name, the historic Three Fingers fire lookout actually sits on the South Peak, not here — the North Peak is a separate, harder objective and is widely considered (though not unanimously, per conflicting elevation surveys) the true high point of the mountain. There is no maintained trail, no ladders, and no register cabin; it's a roped alpine scramble/climb reached via glacier travel from Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap, with genuine exposure and no easy bail once committed to the upper chimney.
backups.beta: Parties typically combine this with the South Peak lookout climb in a single trip since both share the same long approach. From Camp Saddle/Tin Can Gap, descend onto the glacier and traverse to the base of the North Peak, then climb the West Couloir to the South Face. One party describes the climbing as Class 4 with one Class 5 move in the chimney, then easing to Class 2 and 3 near the summit — easier than it is sometimes described, with rock character compared to Chimney Rock.
backups.turnaround: Turn around before committing to the crux chimney move if weather, rockfall, or party pace put a safe return to the glacier and long road-walk-out in doubt.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Boulder River Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the approach basin or on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: Saddle Lake / Three Fingers Trailhead (Trail #641)
waypoints.note: Trailhead on Tupso Pass Spur Rd (FR 4160) off FR 41; no permit required, but the access road has a permanent washout past the Canyon Creek bridge that adds miles of foot/bike travel to reach here.

waypoints.name: Saddle Lake
waypoints.note: Soggy subalpine lake with an Everett Mountaineers-built shelter at its meadow edge; camping is banned within 200 ft of the lake and campfires are prohibited from here upward.
waypoints.directions: Follow Trail #641 uphill from the parking area on a steady forest grade, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams on the way. Routefinding is straightforward and the lake arrives as an abrupt soggy opening rather than a viewpoint. Fill bottles here, since this is the last easy water before the alpine part of the route.

waypoints.name: Goat Flats
waypoints.note: Broad open meadow atop the ridge and the standard basecamp for the climb, about 2.5 mi below the lookout; reliable snowmelt tarns nearby but can dry out late season.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly two more miles past the lake, gaining out of the timber and onto the crest of the ridge before the trail opens into subalpine meadow with views west toward Puget Sound. Campfires are prohibited from the lake upward, so plan a stove-only camp when you stop.

waypoints.name: Tin Can Gap
waypoints.note: Trail crisscrosses the ridge to gain this notch; marks the end of maintained tread and the start of technical scrambling toward the peaks.
waypoints.directions: From the meadows the trail contours and climbs about two more miles, crisscrossing the ridge crest as it works north. Snow lies across this stretch well into summer and can bury the tread entirely, so carry an axe and expect to navigate by terrain rather than by trail. The gap gives the first full view of the three summits and the glacier below; do not continue past it without snow gear and routefinding experience, as this is where parties have needed rescue.

waypoints.name: South Peak lookout ladders
waypoints.note: Three wooden ladders rebarred and wired into the rock climb past the South Peak lookout pinnacle; exposed and can be icy early season, and this is the section the descent text means by 'downclimb the ladders.'
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail and drop roughly 400 feet off the far side of the gap on snow or talus onto the upper glacier, then traverse and climb back up to the saddle beneath the South Peak lookout pinnacle. Early in the year this is a straightforward snow descent and re-ascent; later it goes to bare ice with a moat where the snow has pulled away from the rock, and getting on and off the ice is the awkward part. The ladders start from the rock immediately above that saddle.

waypoints.name: Queest-Alb Glacier headwall crossing
waypoints.note: Route drops onto the north side of the ridge near the top of the Queest-Alb Glacier; a slip on the icy headwall runs out toward crevasses lower on the glacier.
waypoints.directions: Continuing to the true summit means leaving the lookout and dropping back off the ridge onto the north side of the glacier, generally by a gully and rocky moraine rather than straight down. Rope up and watch the runout: the slope above the crevassed lower glacier holds ice by late season and a slip does not stop on its own. Most parties turn around at the lookout, so expect no boot track from here on.

waypoints.name: Col between Middle and North Finger
waypoints.note: Traverse across the glacier gains this col between the Middle and North Fingers, the jump-off point for the West Couloir onto North Peak's South Face.
waypoints.directions: Traverse north across the glacier below the Middle Finger, then climb roughly a thousand feet of snow to the notch; the eastern of the gullies leading up takes steps well when it is firm. Crampons and an axe are wanted, and small crevasses open along the traverse as the season goes on. The col is the last flat ground, so sort gear there before starting up the rock.

waypoints.name: North Peak, Three Fingers
waypoints.note: True summit (Class 4, 5.4 variation), topped out via the West Couloir and South Face above the col; descend by reversing the snow slopes, trail, and ladders.
waypoints.directions: From the col climb the West Couloir onto the South Face, starting on loose third and fourth class rock where anyone above will send debris down. Follow the ramp on the ridge to a chimney holding the hardest moves, exposed fourth to low fifth class and worth a rope and a few slings; a direct line on the upper west face is harder still at about 5.4. Above the chimney the angle eases to class 2-3, but a false summit sits short of the real one, so keep going until you find the register. Coming down is two to three rappels through the chimney and ramp section, often off fixed slings of unknown age that should be backed up.

backups.detailed_rack: A light rack — slings and a small selection of cams/nuts — is enough for protecting the short 5th-class chimney move; the rest of the route is unroped scrambling.
pro_tips: Carry an ice axe for the upper snow even in summer
The fixed ladders to the lookout are exposed—move carefully
backups.pro_needs: Minimal gear placements needed, concentrated at the one 5th-class chimney move; considerable exposure on this section warrants a rope even though the technical difficulty is modest.
backups.approach: Start at the Tupso Pass trailhead (end of FR 41) on the Three Fingers-Goat Flats-Saddle Lake Trail #641. The trail climbs through forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams, to Saddle Lake at about 2.5 miles (last reliable, easy water before the alpine section; no camping within 200 ft of the lake and no fires from here on). From Saddle Lake continue roughly 2–2.5 more miles, gaining out of the timber into the open meadows of Goat Flats (~4.5 mi from the TH) — good camps and the last easy tentsites with views to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail contours and climbs about 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2 mi, roughly 3,500-3,800 ft of the day's gain done); this is the last maintained-trail point and the standard high camp/bivy for peak days. Tin Can Gap gives the first real view of the three summits and the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier below. From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier — early season this is a straightforward snow descent, but by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July); crevasses open on the glacier by mid-summer so rope up if traveling as a team when covered. Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak — this climb is on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock and is the route-finding crux of the approach. From the col, the North Peak route follows a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney, with sustained 4th-class and a few low-5th-class (5.0-5.4) exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block; a harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but is avoided by most parties for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, and a rope+harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line off the North Peak summit. Parties describe two to three rappels getting back down through the 4th/low-5th-class chimney-and-ramp section to easier 3rd-class ground above the glacier — plan on a single 60m rope (or two ropes if parties want to link stations in fewer pulls). The first rappel station is commonly an old fixed sling/tat anchor left by previous parties, but it should not be trusted blindly — inspect it or back it up, and be prepared to build natural gear anchors (cams/nuts on horns or cracks) for the remaining stations since fixed gear is inconsistent year to year. After the rappels, downclimb/scramble the remaining 3rd-class terrain back to the col, reverse the ~1,000 ft descent to the glacier, re-cross the Queest-Alb Glacier (watch the moat and any crevasses), climb back up to Tin Can Gap, and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. Rockfall in the chimney/gully and a icy glacier moat are the main descent-specific hazards; a mid-to-late-season descent in soft/rotten snow on the glacier headwall can also be tricky.
backups.bail: Retreat down the West Couloir/South Face to the glacier is straightforward from most points below the crux chimney; once past the roped 5th-class move, downclimbing or a short rappel off gear may be needed to retreat.

pitch_detail.notes: From Tin Can Gap, drop about 400 ft down steep snow onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Early season it is a plain snow descent. By late summer expect hard, slippery snow or bare ice and a moat where the snow meets the rock, so axe and crampons are needed. Crevasses open by midsummer; rope up when they are snow-covered.

Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft to the col between the Middle and North Peaks. In a high-snow year this goes by a snow tongue and a short couloir of about 40° with moats on both sides. In a low-snow year it becomes loose rock and scree. This climb is the route-finding crux of the day.

Above the col, the climbing is sustained 4th class to a chimney that holds the one real 5th-class move. The rock is loose to fair, so place gear and test holds. Grades given range from Class 4 with a single 5th-class move up to a 40 m lead with harder moves for parties that strayed off the easiest line. An old piton marks one variation.

Above the chimney the ground eases along an exposed, knife-edged crest with big drops east and west. Finish up an easy grassy ramp and over a few blocks to the summit. A short extra low-5th step may be needed depending on the line taken. Rope up for the ridge if the party is unsure: the exposure is serious.

itinerary.cal: Best attempted in late summer (Aug-Sep) once the glacier crossing between Tin Can Gap and the Middle/North col is more consolidated and less crevassed; carry a rope, rack, and glacier gear in addition to standard scrambling kit.

approach_variants.name: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.notes: Note the access before anything else: the road up to the historic trailhead has a permanent washout, so the day starts with a long bike or walk past the vehicle gate before the trail proper begins. From the trailhead, the trail climbs through forest to the small lake at about two and a half miles — last easy water, and no fires or camping within two hundred feet of it. Continue up into the open meadows of the flats at about four and a half miles, the best camping on the route, then a further couple of miles to the GAP at roughly six miles, where the maintained tread ends and most parties bivy. The gap gives the first real view of the three summits and of the glacier below them.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Crevasses open on the glacier by midsummer and bare ice with a moat appears late in the season; an axe is a year-round item on this peak.
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the col

approach_variants.baseFinding: From the gap, drop about four hundred feet off-trail down snow and talus onto the glacier, cross it, and CLIMB BACK UP roughly a thousand feet on the far side to the COL BETWEEN THE MIDDLE AND NORTH TOWERS. That col is the base of the climbing, and the thousand-foot re-ascent is the discriminator: this is the only one of the three summits whose route requires you to gain a col before you touch its rock. From the col the line is a RAMP that leads LEFT and then angles RIGHT into a SHALLOW CHIMNEY — the chimney is the check, being the one chimney breaching the block from this col, and it is fourth class with a move or two of low fifth. Above it an exposed fourth-class ridge leads to a grassy ramp and the summit. Negative markers: if you are standing under THREE STACKED WOODEN LADDERS bolted into the rock, you are at the lookout summit at the southern end of the ridge, two towers away; if you have climbed a short face straight off the glacier with no col gained, you are on the middle tower's south face.

climbing_route.label: Descent from Tin Can Gap onto the Queest-Alb Glacier
climbing_route.notes: From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier. Early season this is a straightforward snow descent; by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July). Crevasses open by mid-summer, so rope up as a team when the glacier is snow-covered.

climbing_route.label: Glacier crossing and climb to the Middle-North col
climbing_route.notes: Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak, on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock. This climb is the route-finding crux.

climbing_route.label: Ramp and shallow chimney to the North Peak summit
climbing_route.notes: From the col, follow a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney. Sustained 4th-class with a few low-5th-class exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block. A harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but most parties avoid it for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, rope and harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season.

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.
bivy.water: Reliable through most of the season from the tarns and small streams in the meadows, though the standing water is shallow and warms up late in summer. Treat everything. Later in a dry year the tarns shrink and the better water is the running melt above the flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
bivy.capacity: The main camping area on this approach — several established pockets spread through the meadows and around the tarns. It absorbs a fair number of parties but is genuinely crowded on summer and autumn weekends, and it is the overflow when the lookout is full.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap high camp
bivy.notes: The last flat ground before the glacier, roughly a mile short of the lookout, and the correct camp for a party that wants the summit block early and cold rather than soft. The maintained trail effectively ends here, so everything above is a bootpath, snow and the ladders. Its value is that it puts the glacier crossing and the ladders in the first hour of the day, when the snow is still firm — a real advantage over starting from the meadows two miles back. The cost is exposure: it is a gap, it catches weather, and there is nothing sheltering about it. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin vegetation, and take a hard look at whether the crossing above is in condition before committing to a camp that only makes sense if you go up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only for most of the season, and nothing at all once the snow around the gap has gone. Assume you are melting or carrying from Goat Flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit required. Federal recreation pass to park. Campfires prohibited on this whole stretch of trail; there is no fuel here regardless.
bivy.capacity: A few small pitches on rock and snow at and just below the gap; one or two parties, not a group site

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.
bivy.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation

backups.overview: The Sitkum Glacier is the standard route on Glacier Peak — the most remote of Washington's major volcanoes. There's no technical crux, but the climb is defined by its long wilderness approach: many miles of trail just to reach a high camp, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It's a true backcountry expedition rewarded by solitude and a wild summit.
backups.beta: From Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft), traverse SE onto the Sitkum Glacier and ascend a corridor on its left (climber's) side heading NE toward a saddle near 9,500 ft by Sitkum Spire. From the saddle, follow the pumice ridge toward the summit, staying right of and below the peak, then finish up a snow chute to the top. Crevasse danger is generally minimal and the route rarely steepens significantly.
backups.turnaround: Turn around by early afternoon on summit day; the long descent to a remote camp leaves no margin for late finishes.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Glacier Peak Wilderness; the approach is 9+ trail miles from the nearest paved road. A satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is recommended.
backups.descent: Reverse the route to Boulder Basin camp and the long trail out.

backups.detailed_rack: Glacier rope team: 30–40 m rope, 2–3 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit. Per person: ice axe, crampons, helmet, harness, locking biners.

If the White Chuck River Road/Trail is washed out or closed, most parties instead reach Boulder Basin via the North Fork Sauk Trail to White Pass and a cross-country traverse into the Glacier Peak basins.

backups.pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for the steeper upper snow and crevasse zones.
backups.best_season: Late June through August — snow-covered glacier, melted-out approach trails. Earlier means deep snow on the long approach; later opens crevasses and bares loose rock.
backups.approach: The White Chuck approach described below is effectively gone: White Chuck River Trail #643 has been listed as inaccessible since the 2003 flood, and the White Chuck Road (FR 23) is closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7, about 5 miles of old roadbed short of the old trailhead, beyond which the valley is unmaintained travel with a river ford. Parties now come in from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead instead, climbing to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass and following it north over Red Pass to the Sitkum Creek junction. From the White Chuck River Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of White Chuck River Road/FR 23), follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) upstream through old-growth forest. The trail fords/bridges several tributaries — Pumice Creek, Glacier Creek, and Kennedy Creek — which serve as reliable water sources but can run high with snowmelt in early summer. At about 5.5 miles reach the former Kennedy Hot Springs/Kennedy Guard Station area (~3,300 ft) — still a popular campsite, but the historic hot-springs pool, lodge, and guard station were destroyed and buried by the October 2003 flood/debris flow and were never rebuilt; there is no usable hot pool here. Continue roughly 1.5 miles farther to Sitkum Creek and the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (~3,850 ft). Turn north (left) on the PCT for about a half mile to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft — a common lower camp. From there, leave the maintained trail and follow a steep, unmaintained climbers' path (locally described as 'more like a fisherman's route than a trail') straight up the forested ridge to Boulder Basin (5,500–6,000 ft), where the trees break and the standard high camp sits on heather/rock benches with running water nearby. From camp, ascend snowfields southeast/uphill onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. Note: the White Chuck River Road and Trail sustained major washout damage in the October 2003 floods and has had repeated closures/repairs since — confirm current road-end and trail status with the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest before relying on this approach, as in bad years the effective trailhead moves miles downstream.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/glacier descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the pumice Sitkum ridge back to the ~9,500 ft saddle east of Sitkum Spire, then descend the Sitkum Glacier's upper section, staying in the corridor left of the icefall/rock rib that splits the glacier's lower half, back down to Boulder Basin. Crevasses exist on the Sitkum but are sparse and generally avoidable with standard route-finding; a rope, harness, and a few pickets are still standard kit. From Boulder Basin, follow the steep climbers' path back down to the PCT/White Chuck Trail junction and retrace the White Chuck River Trail to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Boulder Basin (or your high camp) is the bail point; from the upper mountain you retreat to camp. Given the remoteness, there is no quick escape — bailing means the same long walk out.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the White Chuck River Trail about 5.5 miles to the old Kennedy Hot Springs site, then 1.5 miles more to Sitkum Creek and the PCT. Go north on the PCT about half a mile to a forest camp near 4,100 ft, then take the steep, unmaintained climbers' path up the ridge south of Sitkum Creek to Boulder Basin (5,500–6,000 ft), the usual high camp. Confirm road and trail status before going.

From Boulder Basin, head southeast up snowfields, or a climbers' path later in the season, into a wide snow bowl below the glacier. Do not take the left-hand moraine. It leads to an awkward traverse under a wall of loose rock and then across a steep snowfield to get back on line. Scout the entry the evening before if arriving late, and rope up where the snow meets the ice.

Climb slightly south to the corridor beside the rock feature that splits the lower glacier, then trend northeast. Above that gap the angle eases. Aim for the saddle near 9,500 ft just east of Sitkum Spire, the obvious rock finger on the west summit ridge. Crevasses are not abundant but include hidden ones, even low down, and late season turns stretches to bare ice. Leave camp early, before the snow softens.

From the saddle, follow the pumice ridge toward the summit block. The footing is loose and tiring with no technical difficulty, and most parties unrope here. The saddle can be icy or rimed early in the day, so keep crampons handy. Note where you left the glacier: finding that spot again in a whiteout is the key to the descent.

Keep right of and slightly below the summit, traversing pumice or snow to one of several chutes that climb to the top on its right. The alternative turns left across the upper Scimitar Glacier, then climbs steeply right up the summit snow to the top. The summit gully can hold avalanche debris and a steep final headwall after storms. Descend the same way.

road.seasonalGate: The Mountain Loop Highway's Deer Creek to Bedal section is gated through the winter and typically reopens in mid-May; FR 49 can hold snow into early summer in heavy years.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (the historic standard)
approach_variants.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak and the road access has been unreliable for a very long time. The last several miles of FR 23 to the White Chuck trailhead have been reported blocked — at one point with large boulders placed at the turnoff — and reports of the road being driveable and undriveable have alternated over the years. Confirm with the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie forest before relying on it, because in a bad year the effective trailhead moves miles downstream.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.
hazards: unreliable road access to the trailhead over many years
creek fords running high with early-summer snowmelt
steep unmaintained climbers' path with no signage leaving the PCT
crevasses on the Sitkum
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The path that leaves the PCT for Boulder Basin is unsigned and steeper than anything before it — climbers describe it as more of a fisherman's track than a trail. The test is direction, not appearance: the correct path goes STRAIGHT UP the forested ridge. Anything that contours is the PCT or a game trail.

You know you have arrived at the top of it when the trees break: Boulder Basin at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft is heather and rock benches with running water, and it is the standard high camp. If you are still in continuous forest, you are below it, however long the climb has felt.

From camp the route ascends snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum. Rope up at the point the snowfield stops being a slope you can see the bottom of and becomes continuous glacier — there is no rock landmark for this, so the transition is judged on the ground rather than found.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk and the PCT (the reliable alternative)
approach_variants.notes: Because the White Chuck side has been unreliable for years, parties reach this side of the mountain instead from the North Fork Sauk River trailhead, climbing to White Pass on the PCT and then travelling north over Red Pass toward the Glacier Creek and Sitkum ground. It is substantially longer and is chosen for access rather than for the climbing.
hazards: very long approach on the PCT with substantial gain and loss
no signed junction for the climbers' path
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route above is unchanged: the marker is Boulder Basin — trees giving way to heather and rock benches with running water at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft — and then snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum above it. Arriving from the north on the PCT the risk is passing the drainage entirely, so identify the Sitkum Creek and Glacier Creek junctions on the map before you set out rather than expecting signage.

climbing_route.label: Snowfields onto the glacier toe
climbing_route.notes: From the Boulder Basin camp at 5,500-6,000 ft, head southeast up snowfields and moraine to gain the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. This is the one place parties routinely go wrong: taking the left-hand moraine commits you to an awkward traverse beneath a wall of loose rock and then across a steep snowfield to recover the correct line. Sort the entry out in daylight if you can, and rope up before stepping onto glacier ice.

climbing_route.label: Lower glacier corridor
climbing_route.notes: Trend slightly south to take the corridor on the left side of the rock feature that divides the lower glacier, then work back northeast. Both open and hidden crevasses are present here and the crossing points shift year to year and even week to week, so expect to weave and to reverse a line or two. Late-season melt-out exposes more bare ice and pushes the practical route further off any recorded track — a GPS trace from a previous party is a hint, not a route.

climbing_route.label: Upper glacier to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: Continue northeast up the upper glacier to a saddle at roughly 9,500 ft just east of Sitkum Spire. The firn line on the upper glacier has been retreating and bare ice is increasingly exposed, which makes crampons and a firmer belay standard rather than optional in late summer. A bergschrund sits below the saddle and is the last crevasse hazard on the ascent. This is a shaded, exposed slope late in the day — softening snow after mid-morning is the reason parties leave camp in the small hours.

climbing_route.label: Sitkum Ridge pumice
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, leave the glacier for the pumice of Sitkum Ridge. This is loose, ball-bearing volcanic debris on a moderate slope — no technical difficulty, but tiring underfoot and easy to send rock down onto anyone behind. Most parties unrope here. Being off the glacier, it is also the point where a whiteout descent becomes hard to navigate by feel, so mark the spot where you leave the snow.

climbing_route.label: Summit slope
climbing_route.notes: Stay to the right of and slightly below the summit as you gain height, then take the snow chute that leads up to the top. The whole route is a glacier and snow climb with no rock pitches, but it is a long day at altitude on an isolated volcano where weather closes in quickly and the descent retraces every crevasse crossing made on the way up.

bivy.name: Boulder Basin
bivy.notes: The standard planned high camp, in an open meadow basin at the treeline with the glacier toe above. It is a pleasant place — flowers, waterfalls, and correspondingly aggressive marmots and bugs — but earning it means a long approach and then a steep, unmaintained climbers' path straight up a forested ridge with a full pack. It is about ten miles from the road end, and the road itself has a long history of washouts, so confirm where the trailhead actually is before you plan the day.
bivy.water: Waterfalls and snowmelt streams run through the basin; dependable into late summer but shrinking as the season goes on. Filter it
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit is required for overnight use in this wilderness
bivy.capacity: Several established sites on heather and rock benches at treeline, spread through the basin between roughly 5,500 and 6,000 ft

bivy.name: Kennedy Guard Station area
bivy.notes: The lowest planned stop, about 5.5 miles in and still widely used. Do not plan on soaking: the historic hot pool, lodge and guard station here were buried by the 2003 flood and debris flow and were never rebuilt. Useful as a first night for parties splitting the approach, or as a retreat in bad weather, but it is a long way and a lot of gain below the glacier.

bivy.name: Sitkum Creek / PCT junction camp
bivy.notes: A lower fallback for parties who run out of daylight on the long walk in, sitting where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail. Below treeline, so it is sheltered and out of the weather, but it leaves the entire steep climbers' path plus 1,500 ft of gain before you are even at the standard camp.
bivy.capacity: A small forested site or two just north of the trail junction
